opening.headline: When a service depends on a single model, you learn how to plan the order of checks and how to roll back, including the methods to implement such changes when there are 50 such services.
body: When the provider announces the model retirement schedule, all services using that model must update simultaneously. If there's only one service, it can be updated individually; however, if fifty services depend on the same model ID, the situation changes. Updating them all at once means a single error affects all fifty services at the same time.

In this course, we start from the service inventory and classify services along two axes: impact and risk, learning how to develop a transition plan that includes evaluation gates, staged deployment, and rollback procedures. Finally, we examine a case study on how to prioritize when services with near-expiry dates overlap with high-risk services.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Services can be classified along two axes: impact and risk.
Can assess whether the transition plan includes evaluation gates and staged deployments.

screens.title: 50 services depend on one model
screens.lead: First, read about the challenges that arise when there are many services dependent on the same model.

visual.alt: Five services extend arrows from a single model ID, with an expiration date pressing from above.
labels: Model ID: Model with a specified expiration date

paragraphs: Let's assume that 50 services within the company depend on the same model ID. Suppose the provider has announced the end-of-life schedule for that model, and after the end date, the model can no longer be invoked. All 50 services must be migrated to a new model before the end date.

While it may seem quick to make changes all at once, a single mistake can spread across 50 services simultaneously. Each service has its own considerations. The impact on users, regulatory burdens, responsible teams, and the ability to make changes all vary from one service to another.
The three questions to be answered in this class are: In what order will we proceed? What checkpoints will we use to move to the next stage? And how will we revert if a problem arises?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Just because the end date is the same does not mean all services must operate in the same order or manner.

screens.outro: First, let's consider what comes to mind as a criterion for determining order.

screens.title: How do you determine the order for replacing models?
screens.lead: When you select one of the three candidate criteria, the instructor's thought process becomes clear. First, think mentally about which criterion fits best, then click it to select. The answer is neither entered nor submitted.

items.prompt: Candidate Criterion 1: Change services with nearer end dates first
items.answer: Expiration dates are clearly important constraints. However, relying solely on expiration dates to determine order may result in the most risky services being changed without preparation, simply because they have earlier expiration dates. In this course, we treat expiration dates not as the primary criterion for ordering, but rather as constraints that push start times forward.

items.prompt: Candidate Criterion 2: The user starts by changing the service that they use the most.
items.answer: Services used by many users cause significant damage when they fail, and changing the most impactful service without prior transition experience is a risky choice.

items.prompt: Candidate Criterion 3: Start by changing services that have little impact even if they fail.
items.answer: This is the benchmark closest to the conclusion of this course. First, learn where evaluation bundles, prompt tuning, and parameter adjustments break down in low-cost failure scenarios, and then proactively apply that experience to higher-risk services.

screens.outro: Now we will examine how to classify services by impact and risk.

screens.title: From Inventory to Classification: The Grid of Impact and Risk
screens.lead: When you select a number marker, you can view detailed descriptions of each grid cell and the classification criteria.

visual.alt: A four-cell grid divided along the axes of impact and risk, along with the service inventory table to its left.
labels: Classification result + Provider termination date = Service-specific deadline

markers.label: Service Inventory
markers.title: The first step is inventory.
markers.body: The starting point of classification is the service inventory. The service, model ID, call path, owner, and expiration date must be present in a single table. Since service termination notices are issued at the model level, the absence of this table makes it difficult to determine which services are affected.

markers.label: No impact, low risk
markers.title: Pilot candidate panel
markers.body: A service with minimal user impact and low transition risk is a pilot candidate. For example, a tool used exclusively by internal staff fits this category. Here, we first transition to evaluate the bundle and prompt adjustments, and identify where parameter changes break.

markers.label: Impact is significant, risk is low
markers.title: Low-risk, high-impact services
markers.body: The user impact is significant, but the prompt is simple and includes predefined evaluation criteria, resulting in low conversion risk. Apply the checklist learned from the pilot and proceed with phased deployment. Due to the high impact, clearly define rollback conditions.

markers.label: Impact: Yes, Risk: High
markers.title: High-risk, low-impact services
markers.body: The impact is small, but services that heavily use tool calls or rely on prefill and sampling values pose higher transition risks. Due to the low impact, failure would incur minimal cost, making it a suitable second pilot for learning and understanding risks.

markers.label: Impact is significant, risk is high
markers.title: Final step
markers.body: Services with significant impact and high risk are moved last, after being thoroughly prepared and ready. They must be in a state that includes all the evaluation bundles, checklists, and rollback conditions accumulated from the earlier stages.

screens.outro: Since we have confirmed the classification criteria, let's now examine the specific rationale for assessing risks.

screens.title: Transition order and evaluation gates
screens.lead: Select each tab to verify the order of transitions and how the evaluation gates operate.

tabs.label: Basis for reading risks
tabs.body:
**Impact Axis** evaluates based on user face-to-face interaction, regulatory status, and damage incurred when operations are halted.

**Risk Axis** evaluates based on prompt complexity, tool calling usage, possession of evaluation bundles, and model parameter dependency. The Claude model transition guide lists thinking budget, sampling parameters, assistant prefill, and forced tool choice as causes of error 400. Whether the service code depends on such settings constitutes specific evidence for risk classification.

tabs.label: Transition order
tabs.body:
The overall order is **inventory, classification, pilot, expansion**.

Pilots consist of services with low risk and minimal impact. Expansion gradually broadens the scope to areas with increasing impact. Each stage begins by reflecting the lessons learned from the previous stage into a checklist.

tabs.label: evaluation gate
tabs.body:
The evaluation gate is a checkpoint that compares a baseline and a new model using the same input batch, and only sends services that pass the evaluation to the next stage.

OpenAI's evaluation best practices document explains that evaluations should be conducted early and frequently, with continuous evaluations run after every change, and that evaluation data must reflect the patterns of actual operational traffic. It also identifies post-launch "seemingly plausible" evaluations as an anti-pattern.

tabs.label: Gate Design
tabs.body:
The document recommends that LLMs are better at distinguishing between options, and thus evaluation should be conducted through methods such as pairwise comparison, classification, or criteria-based scoring rather than open-ended generation.

Gate criteria are adjusted according to the risk level of the service. The key point is to **establish pass conditions before viewing the results**. If criteria are defined after seeing the results, the gate will effectively do nothing.

screens.outro: We will look at how actually deploying and rolling back services that have passed through the gate.

screens.title: Staged Deployment and Rollback
screens.lead: Examine the traffic ratio sent to a new model by gradually moving the slider. The ratio is illustrative and intended to explain the flow.

visual.alt: The traffic ratio moving to the new model is increasing step by step, with the rollback path shown below in the diagram.
labels: Rollback: Return to previous model ID
Rollback conditions: degradation in evaluation metrics, increase in error rate

data.controlLabel: Traffic ratio sent to the new model

stops.body: Only a portion of traffic is sent to the new model. Few users are affected in case of issues, and you can first observe the actual input differences that previously were not visible in evaluation batches. At this stage, you examine error rates, unusual response formats, and evaluation metrics.

If the metric is stable, it widens the range. At this stage, the metrics of the previous model and the new model are compared side by side. If a signal indicating a rollback condition is detected, the ratio is immediately reduced.

Even if half of the data is migrated to the new model, the previous model path remains active, allowing rollback at any time. Since the previous model can only be used until the expiration date, the rollback period is reflected in the schedule to end on the expiration date.

All traffic has been migrated to the new model. However, the previous model path is not immediately deleted but retained as a rollback path until the end-of-life date. Rollback conditions are determined solely by predefined criteria established before deployment, such as a decline in evaluation metrics or an increase in error rates.

screens.outro: Now let's follow through with an example to understand why we start transitioning from services with low risk.

screens.title: Explanation: Why transition starting from low-risk services
screens.lead: The instructor breaks down the transition order of the three services step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: case
steps.body: Internal summarization tool, internal document search, and customer service bot are all using the same model. All three services must reach their end date simultaneously. Which service should we switch first?

steps.title: Pilot internal summary tool
steps.body: Internal summary tools have little impact on internal staff, and issues can be quickly detected and resolved. Therefore, they are well-suited for pilot programs. When selecting a pilot, consider whether it is easy to create evaluation bundles and whether the responsible team has the capacity to cooperate. The most important condition is that business operations do not halt even if the service fails.

steps.title: Learns where the failure occurs in the pilot
steps.body: Checks whether the evaluation bundle is useful in the pilot, how far the prompt needs to be tuned, and where parameter changes cause issues. This learning is the most important outcome of this stage. Here, issues such as post-processing breaking when the prompt format changes or prefill settings causing 400 errors first become apparent.

steps.title: Reflected in the checklist and disseminated
steps.body: Reflect learned points in a checklist and disseminate them through internal document search. This helps avoid repeating the same mistakes. Since this service has a broader impact, it uses a phased rollout approach.

steps.title: The customer service bot is moved last.
steps.body: The customer service bot transitions only after accumulating a set of evaluated feedback and meeting rollback conditions. Since failure would immediately impact the customer, the most preparation is required.

steps.title: reason
steps.body: This is to apply knowledge gained in low-cost-failure environments to high-cost-failure environments. The principle of this sequence is to learn in low-risk areas and then move to high-risk areas.

screens.outro: But if the shutdown date for a high-risk service is the closest, what will happen then? Let's explore this further.

screens.title: Explanation: Conflict resolution between expiration date order and sequence
screens.lead: Compare how the order is changed when transitioning between two states and a conflict occurs.

states.label: Collision scenario
states.body:
Customer service bots are high-risk but have the closest expiration date. If moved based on risk criteria, they won't align with the expiration date; if moved based on expiration date criteria, they'll be underprepared.

The two criteria are directly conflicting. In such cases, either rushing to move while ignoring risk or delaying while ignoring the expiration date are not viable options. After the expiration date, prior models can no longer be invoked. Therefore, the solution is not to reverse the entire order, but rather to advance the preparation work for high-risk services.

states.label: Adjustment method
states.body:
**Adjustment 1**: Work backward from the termination date to establish the timeframe required for evaluation, re-evaluation, and phased rollout.

**Adjustment 2**: Begin preparing evaluation bundles for high-risk services early, in parallel with the pilot phase. By accelerating this preparation, you can align the schedule without altering the sequence.

**Adjustment 3**: If the schedule still does not align, contact the vendor’s support channel to inquire about extending the timeframe or allocating additional capacity. OpenAI documentation indicates that in certain cases, dedicated capacity may be available for access after termination, and it recommends contacting the sales team.

**Decision**: The sequence is prioritized by risk, and the termination date is treated as a constraint that limits the start date.

For example, if there are still three months until termination and two months are required for evaluation, re-evaluation, and phased rollout of the customer support bot, the process must begin no later than one month from termination. If the backward-calculated start date is earlier than the pilot schedule, the evaluation bundle preparation is conducted concurrently with the pilot.

screens.outro: I will now consolidate and summarize the previous components into a single section.

screens.title: One-page summary of transition plan components
screens.lead: Read the table from top to bottom and review what each of the five elements of the transition plan determines.

data.caption: Components of a multi-service model migration plan
rows: Divide services along two axes: impact and risk. Impact is assessed based on user interaction, regulation, and scale of damage. Risk is evaluated based on prompt complexity, tool calling, evaluation bundles, and parameter dependency.
It proceeds in order from low-risk to high-risk locations. The end date is adjusted to reflect the constraint of advancing the start time.
This is a pass condition that compares the baseline with a new model using the same input batch. The pass condition is defined before viewing the results.
Before the start of any service transition
A plan to gradually scale out by distributing traffic, along with metrics observed at each stage.
After passing through the gate, before deployment
Path and conditions to revert to a previous model ID. For example, a decline in evaluation metrics or an increase in error rate. The previous model can be used only until termination.
data.notes: The five elements are interlinked. Classification establishes order, order determines the strength of gates and deployment, and rollback conditions must be defined prior to deployment to function effectively. Google Well-Architected's AI/ML perspective also provides principles that jointly guide consideration of operational excellence, security, reliability, cost, and performance.

glossary.def: This is a task of categorizing services along two axes: user impact and transition risk.
The new model must satisfy a predefined criterion relative to the baseline in order to meet the pass condition and proceed to the next stage.
This is a method where a portion of traffic is sent to a new model, thereby expanding the scope.
This is the path to revert to the previous model settings when an issue occurs.
This is the initial stage where you transition first in a low-risk service to learn about the issues.

misconceptions.myth: It's faster and safer to update everything at once.
misconceptions.fact: A single error can propagate across all services simultaneously. It's safer to start with low-risk areas and gradually expand.

misconceptions.myth: The effect is significant only when the user engages with many services.
misconceptions.fact: Services with high failure costs should be migrated after being learned from. First, validation of evaluation bundles and reconfiguration methods should occur in areas with minimal impact.

misconceptions.myth: Rollback can be considered after a problem has occurred.
misconceptions.fact: The rollback path and conditions must be established prior to deployment. Since the previous model only allowed specifying an expiration date, a rollback period must also be considered and reflected in the schedule.

closing.lead: This summarizes the core content of the class.
points: Start learning in low-risk areas and move to higher-risk areas.
The evaluation gate and rollback conditions are defined before deployment.
The end date is a constraint that advances the start point.
closing.reflectionLead: The questions below are for your own reflection only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What service should be prioritized in our organization's transition, and why was that service chosen?
